title: Social Media Exposure to Cannabis and Vaping Content Drives Teen Substance Use, Study Finds
excerpt: Research published in JAMA Network Open found that high school students frequently exposed to cannabis and e-cigarette posts on social media were significantly more likely to initiate substance use within a year.
body:
• Adolescents frequently exposed to cannabis-related social media content were up to 83% more likely to initiate e-cigarette use and 71% more likely to start dual substance use within one year.
  • Content from friends and microinfluencers had the strongest association with teen substance use, while celebrity and brand posts showed no significant link.
  • TikTok emerged as a particularly influential platform, with frequent exposure to e-cigarette content on the app linked to higher rates of cannabis and dual use.
  • Nearly 77% of substance-related content on social media portrays use in a positive light, according to a review of 73 studies.

Teenagers who regularly encounter cannabis and e-cigarette content on social media are significantly more likely to start using these substances, according to a large-scale study published in JAMA Network Open that tracked more than 7,600 California high school students.

The research, led by investigators from the University of Southern California, Rutgers University, and the University of Oklahoma, adds to a mounting body of evidence linking social media exposure to adolescent risk behaviors — and identifies which platforms and content sources carry the most influence.

From Scrolling to Substance Use

The first component of the study followed 4,232 high school students who had never used e-cigarettes or cannabis at baseline. Nearly 23% reported seeing e-cigarette-related posts on social media at least weekly, while 12% reported similar exposure to cannabis content. On TikTok specifically, 13.4% of students encountered e-cigarette content weekly or more.

One year later, 3.6% had started using e-cigarettes alone, 3.9% had initiated cannabis use alone, and 4.5% had begun using both substances.

Frequent exposure to cannabis-related social media posts was significantly associated with all three outcomes. According to the study, cannabis content exposure was linked to an adjusted odds ratio of 1.83 for solo e-cigarette use, 1.60 for solo cannabis use, and 1.71 for dual use initiation.

TikTok proved especially potent. Frequent exposure to e-cigarette posts on the platform was associated with a 74% higher likelihood of solo cannabis use and a 78% higher likelihood of dual use, according to the researchers.

Friends and Microinfluencers Matter Most

A second, cross-sectional survey of 3,380 students examined whether the source of the content mattered. It did — substantially.

Posts from friends and microinfluencers showed the strongest links to substance use. Adolescents exposed to e-cigarette content from microinfluencers had an adjusted odds ratio of 2.67 for past-month cannabis use. Exposure to friends' cannabis posts was linked to cannabis use with an odds ratio of 3.35 and dual use at 2.46.

"Since exposure to e-cigarette or cannabis posts may contribute to adolescent e-cigarette, cannabis, or dual use, improvement of social media community guidelines and greater policy attention to co-use and marketing of e-cigarettes and cannabis may help prevent youth substance use."

— Study authors, JAMA Network Open

Celebrity and brand posts, by contrast, showed no significant association with past-month e-cigarette use. Content from unknown or unidentifiable sources was similarly ineffective.

A Wider Pattern of Risk

The findings align with broader research connecting social media use to adolescent substance experimentation. A separate study published in The American Journal of Psychiatry found that adolescents who began using social media early and rapidly increased their use were far more likely to experiment with alcohol, tobacco, and cannabis.

That research, led by Dr. Jason Nagata at the University of California, San Francisco, found that the heaviest early users had nearly 17 times the odds of experimenting with cannabis and 14 times the odds of trying tobacco compared with peers who reported little or no social media use.

A review of 73 studies found that nearly 77% of substance-related content on social media portrays use positively, according to CNN's reporting on the research. Alcohol marketing is pervasive, with one study documenting nearly 40,000 alcohol ads placed on Facebook and Instagram over a single year in Australia.

What Experts Recommend

The American Academy of Pediatrics advocates for a balanced approach: setting boundaries while guiding children through media literacy. Its "5 C's" framework emphasizes tailoring care to the individual child, monitoring content, providing calming alternatives to screens, understanding how phone use crowds out family time, and starting conversations early.

"Don't wait until there's a problem," Nagata told CNN. "It's important to be proactive if your child is going to be on social media."

The JAMA study was funded by the National Institutes of Health and the National Institute on Drug Abuse.
